findings.description: os.system uses an f-string to build a shell command from the `directory` parameter; if an attacker can control this value, it enables arbitrary command injection and dangerous recursive deletion. The immutable `rm -rf` compound command further increases data-loss risk.

subprocess.call is invoked with shell=True and an f-string containing `path` and `host`; this is a direct command-injection path that can execute arbitrary shell commands. Static evidence marks this as AST_DANGEROUS_SUBPROCESS_SHELL high at line 8.
os.popen directly executes arbitrary user input as a shell command; this is arbitrary command execution and should never be used with untrusted input.

fix_description: Replace all three dangerous shell-execution paths with safe, non-shell APIs and input validation. (1) cleanup_old_files: do not use os.system with an f-string; instead build an absolute path with pathlib and delete only the intended directory contents using e.g. Path(directory).glob('*') with unlink/unlink_dir, or use shutil.rmtree only after validating that directory is an expected absolute/relative path and rejecting empty or root values. (2) run_backup: replace subprocess.call(..., shell=True) with subprocess.run([...], shell=False) using a fixed argument list, e.g. ['scp', '-r', path_arg, f'user@{host}:/backup'], and validate/escape host/path as parameters rather than interpolating into a shell string. (3) execute_command: replace os.popen(user_input) with a whitelist/allowlist of permitted commands and parse input as structured arguments; if arbitrary shell execution is truly required, reject untrusted input and execute via subprocess.run(list_args, shell=False) with no_such_shell. All changes preserve intended functionality while eliminating command injection and recursive-deletion risk. These are auto-fixable for a review patch, but deployment to critical environments should still be human-reviewed due to the invasive behavior change.
